title: Excretory Products and Their Elimination
syllabus: Modes of excretion - Ammonotelism, ureotelism, uricotelism; Human excretory system - structure and function; Urine formation, Osmoregulation; Regulation of kidney function - Renin-angiotensin, Atrial Natriuretic Factor, ADH and Diabetes insipidus; Role of other organs in excretion; Disorders - Uraemia, Renal failure, Renal calculi, Nephritis; Dialysis and artificial kidney.

questions.question: Which of the following nitrogenous wastes is the most toxic and requires the maximum amount of water for its elimination from the body?
questions.solution: Ammonia is the most toxic nitrogenous waste product and requires large volumes of water for its elimination. It is excreted by aquatic invertebrates, bony fishes, and aquatic amphibians (ammonotelic animals).

questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II regarding the modes of nitrogenous excretion and representative animal groups:

List-I (Excretory Mode)List-II (Representative Animals)
(A) Ammonotelism(I) Mammals, terrestrial amphibians, and marine fishes
(B) Ureotelism(II) Reptiles, birds, land snails, and insects
(C) Uricotelism(III) Aquatic amphibians, bony fishes, and aquatic insects

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.solution: Ammonotelism: Aquatic amphibians, bony fishes, aquatic insects; Ureotelism: Mammals, terrestrial amphibians, marine cartilaginous fishes; Uricotelism: Reptiles, birds, terrestrial snails, insects (excrete uric acid paste/pellets with minimum water loss).

questions.question: In the human kidney, specialized epithelial cells of the visceral layer of Bowman's capsule that form intricate filtration slits (slit pores) are called:
questions.solution: Podocytes are specialized epithelial cells of the visceral layer of Bowman's capsule arranged in an intricate manner to leave minute spaces called filtration slits or slit pores across the glomerular filtration membrane.

questions.question: The Glomerular Filtration Rate (GFR) in a healthy adult human is approximately:
questions.solution: The amount of filtrate formed by both kidneys per minute is called GFR. In a healthy human, GFR is approximately $125\text{ mL/minute}$, which amounts to $180\text{ litres}$ per day.

questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II regarding the segments of a Nephron and their localized transport functions:

List-I (Nephron Segment)List-II (Transport Characteristic)
(A) Proximal Convoluted Tubule (PCT)(I) Impermeable to water; actively transports $\text{NaCl}$ into medullary interstitium
(B) Descending limb of loop of Henle(II) Reabsorbs nearly $70-80\%$ of electrolytes and water; brush-bordered
(C) Ascending limb of loop of Henle(III) Permeable to water but almost impermeable to electrolytes
(D) Distal Convoluted Tubule (DCT)(IV) Conditional reabsorption of $\text{Na}^+$ and water under aldosterone/ADH

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.solution: PCT: Reabsorbs $70-80\%$ of filtered electrolytes, glucose, and water; Descending limb: Permeable to water, concentrates filtrate; Ascending limb: Impermeable to water, dilutes filtrate by extruding $\text{NaCl}$; DCT: Conditional reabsorption of $\text{Na}^+$ and $\text{H}_2\text{O}$.

questions.question: The counter-current mechanism that helps maintain an increasing hyperosmolar medullary interstitial gradient operates between which two structures?
options: Two limbs of the Loop of Henle and Vasa Recta
questions.solution: The counter-current mechanism operates due to opposite flow directions in the two limbs of Henle's loop and the two limbs of the vasa recta, establishing an increasing medullary osmolarity gradient from $300\text{ mOsmol/L}$ in the cortex to $1200\text{ mOsmol/L}$ in the inner medulla.

questions.question: Which of the following two substances primarily maintain the increasing medullary interstitial hyperosmolarity in mammalian kidneys?
questions.solution: $\text{NaCl}$ transported by the ascending limb of Henle's loop (exchanged with vasa recta) and small amounts of urea diffusing out of the lower collecting duct maintain the osmotic gradient in the medullary interstitium.

questions.question:
Read the following statements regarding the Juxtaglomerular Apparatus (JGA):
Statement I: JGA is a specialized cellular structure formed by cellular modifications at the location of contact between the DCT and the afferent arteriole.
Statement II: A fall in glomerular filtration rate (GFR) activates the juxtaglomerular (JG) cells to release renin.

Choose the correct option:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct
questions.solution: Both statements are correct according to NCERT. JGA comprises the macula densa (in DCT) and renin-secreting JG cells (in afferent arteriole). A fall in GFR/blood pressure stimulates JG cells to release renin into circulation.

questions.question: The Renin-Angiotensin-Aldosterone System (RAAS) regulates blood pressure. Renin converts:
options: Angiotensinogen in blood to Angiotensin I
questions.solution: Renin is an aspartyl protease secreted by JG cells that converts plasma angiotensinogen (produced by liver) into angiotensin I, which is converted to angiotensin II by ACE in pulmonary capillaries.

questions.question: Atrial Natriuretic Factor (ANF) is secreted by the atria of the heart in response to an increase in blood pressure/volume. ANF functions to:
options: Cause vasodilation and increase excretion of $\text{Na}^+$, thereby decreasing blood pressure (antagonist to RAAS)
Cause powerful vasoconstriction and stimulate aldosterone release
Stimulate release of renin from JG cells
Promote water retention in collecting duct
questions.solution: An increase in blood flow to the atria causes release of ANF. ANF causes vasodilation of blood vessels and promotes natriuresis ($\text{Na}^+$ excretion), which reduces blood pressure, acting as a check on the RAAS.

questions.question: Deficiency of Anti-Diuretic Hormone (ADH / Vasopressin) or unresponsiveness of kidneys to ADH leads to which of the following disorders?
options: Diabetes insipidus (excessive excretion of dilute urine)
questions.solution: Deficiency of ADH (or its receptor resistance) impairs water reabsorption in the DCT and collecting duct, leading to excessive loss of dilute urine (polyuria) and extreme thirst (polydipsia), known as Diabetes insipidus.

questions.question: Which of the following accessory excretory organs eliminates bilirubin, biliverdin, cholesterol, degraded steroid hormones, vitamins, and drugs through digestive wastes?
questions.solution: The liver is the largest digestive/excretory gland that degrades hemoglobin into bile pigments (bilirubin and biliverdin), secretes cholesterol, altered steroids, and drugs, and eliminates them along with digestive fecal wastes.

questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II regarding the excretory roles of human accessory organs:

List-I (Excretory Organ)List-II (Eliminated Waste Substances)
(A) Lungs(I) Sterols, hydrocarbons, and waxes in sebum
(B) Sweat glands(II) Approximately $200\text{ mL/minute}$ of $\text{CO}_2$ and significant amounts of water
(C) Sebaceous glands(III) Water, $\text{NaCl}$, small amounts of urea, and lactic acid

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.solution: Lungs: Eliminate $\text{CO}_2$ (approx. $200\text{ mL/min}$ or $18\text{ L/day}$) and water vapor; Sweat glands: Eliminate $\text{NaCl}$, urea, lactic acid; Sebaceous glands: Eliminate sterols, hydrocarbons, and waxes.

questions.question: An accumulation of high levels of urea in blood due to kidney malfunction is clinically termed:
questions.solution: Malfunction of kidneys can lead to an accumulation of urea in blood, a pathological condition called uraemia, which is highly toxic and may cause acute renal failure.

questions.question: Renal calculi are commonly described as:
options: Stones or insoluble crystallized masses of salts (like calcium oxalates) formed within the kidney
Inflammation of the glomeruli of kidney
Rupture of collecting ducts due to high pressure
questions.solution: Renal calculi (kidney stones) are insoluble crystallized stones or masses of salts, such as calcium oxalate or uric acid crystals, deposited within the renal calyces or pelvis.

questions.question: Glomerulonephritis is defined pathologically as:
options: Inflammation of the glomeruli of the kidney
questions.solution: Glomerulonephritis is an inflammatory disease affecting the glomeruli of the kidneys, often mediated by immune complexes.

questions.question: In a hemodialysis unit (artificial kidney), which anticoagulant is added to the patient's blood before pumping it into the dialyzing unit?
questions.solution: Blood drained from a convenient artery is pumped into a dialyzing unit after adding an anticoagulant like heparin. Before returning cleared blood to a vein, anti-heparin is added.

questions.question: The dialyzing fluid in a hemodialysis machine has the exact same composition as plasma EXCEPT that it lacks:
questions.solution: The dialyzing fluid has the same composition as normal blood plasma except for the absence of nitrogenous wastes. This concentration gradient allows metabolic wastes (urea, creatinine) to diffuse freely out of blood through the cellophane membrane.

questions.question: Out of the $180\text{ litres}$ of glomerular filtrate produced daily in an adult human, what percentage is reabsorbed by the renal tubules?
questions.solution: Out of the $180\text{ L}$ of filtrate formed per day, the urine released is only about $1.5\text{ L}$, which means that nearly $99\%$ of the glomerular filtrate is reabsorbed by the renal tubular epithelium.

questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II regarding the tubular handling of different substances across nephrons:

List-I (Substance)List-II (Mechanism of Tubular Transport)
(A) Glucose and Amino acids(I) Passive diffusion
(B) Nitrogenous wastes (Urea)(II) Active transport
(C) $\text{H}^+$ and $\text{K}^+$ ions(III) Active tubular secretion

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.solution: Glucose and amino acids: Active reabsorption in PCT ($100\%$); Nitrogenous wastes like urea: Passive transport; $\text{H}^+, \text{K}^+,$ and ammonia: Active tubular secretion into filtrate to maintain ionic and acid-base balance.

questions.question: Cortical nephrons differ from Juxtamedullary nephrons because Cortical nephrons have:
options: Short loops of Henle extending only very little into the medulla, with poorly developed vasa recta
Long loops of Henle running deep into the inner medulla with well-developed vasa recta
Glomeruli located in the renal pelvis
questions.solution: In cortical nephrons (majority, ~85%), the loop of Henle is short and extends only very little into the medulla, and vasa recta is absent or reduced. In juxtamedullary nephrons (~15%), the loop of Henle is long and extends deep into the medulla with well-developed vasa recta.

questions.question: A notched indentation on the inner concave surface of the kidney through which the ureter, blood vessels, and nerves enter is called the:
questions.solution: Towards the centre of the inner concave border of the kidney is a notch called the hilum (or hilus) through which the ureter, renal blood vessels, lymphatics, and nerves enter.

questions.question: Renal columns of Bertini are extensions of:
questions.solution: The renal cortex extends inwards between the conical medullary pyramids as prominent columns called renal columns of Bertini.

questions.question: The diameter of the efferent arteriole is narrower than that of the afferent arteriole. This structural difference creates:
options: High glomerular hydrostatic pressure necessary for ultrafiltration
Low pressure to allow passive diffusion only
Retrograde flow of blood to the renal artery
questions.solution: The efferent arteriole has a narrower lumen than the afferent arteriole, which generates high hydrostatic pressure (~60 mm Hg) inside the glomerular capillary network to drive ultrafiltration.

questions.question:
Read the following statements regarding Micturition:
Statement I: The neural mechanism that causes the release of urine is called the micturition reflex.
Statement II: Stretch receptors on the urinary bladder wall send signals to the CNS when the bladder fills, triggering parasympathetic contraction of the detrusor muscle and relaxation of the urethral sphincter.

Choose the correct option:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct
questions.solution: Both statements are correct according to NCERT. Filling of the urinary bladder stretches the detrusor wall; stretch receptors generate signals to the CNS, initiating autonomic motor impulses that contract the bladder and relax the sphincter, causing urination (micturition).

questions.question: On an average, an adult human excretes how much urine and how much urea per day respectively?
options: $1.0 - 1.5\text{ litres}$ of urine and $25 - 30\text{ grams}$ of urea
$2.5 - 3.0\text{ litres}$ of urine and $50\text{ grams}$ of urea
$0.5\text{ litres}$ of urine and $10\text{ grams}$ of urea
$5.0\text{ litres}$ of urine and $5\text{ grams}$ of urea
questions.solution: An adult human eliminates on average $1.0 - 1.5\text{ litres}$ of urine per day containing about $25 - 30\text{ grams}$ of urea.

questions.question: Analysis of urine shows the presence of glucose (Glycosuria) and ketone bodies (Ketonuria). These clinical indicators are diagnostic of:
questions.solution: Presence of glucose (glycosuria) and ketone bodies (ketonuria) in urine is indicative of uncontrolled Diabetes mellitus (insulin deficiency causing hyperglycemia and fat breakdown).

questions.question: Osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus are activated by changes in:
options: Blood volume, body fluid volume, and ionic/osmolar concentration
Carbon dioxide partial pressure in alveoli
questions.solution: Hypothalamic osmoreceptors are stimulated by an increase in blood osmolarity or a decrease in blood volume/body fluid volume, prompting the release of ADH (vasopressin) from the neurohypophysis.

questions.question: Angiotensin II restores GFR by which of the following mechanisms?
options: Acts as a powerful vasoconstrictor to raise glomerular blood pressure and stimulates adrenal cortex to release aldosterone
questions.solution: Angiotensin II is a powerful vasoconstrictor that raises glomerular capillary blood pressure (increasing GFR) and stimulates the adrenal cortex to secrete aldosterone (promoting $\text{Na}^+$ and water reabsorption in the DCT).

questions.question: Human urine is typically slightly acidic with an average pH value of:
questions.solution: Human urine is a transparent, light yellow watery fluid that is slightly acidic, with an average pH of approximately 6.0 (range 4.5–8.0).

questions.question: In terrestrial reptiles and birds, nitrogenous waste is converted into uric acid primarily to:
options: Conserve body water, as uric acid is insoluble and excreted as a semi-solid paste
questions.solution: Uric acid is the least toxic nitrogenous waste and is practically insoluble in water. Reptiles, birds, and insects excrete uric acid as a semi-solid pellet or paste with minimum water loss, which is an adaptation for terrestrial life.

questions.question: Human kidneys are positioned retroperitoneally between the levels of which vertebrae?
options: Last thoracic (T12) and third lumbar (L3) vertebrae
questions.solution: In humans, the kidneys are reddish-brown, bean-shaped organs situated between the levels of the last thoracic (T12) and third lumbar (L3) vertebrae, attached to the dorsal inner abdominal wall.

questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II regarding the parts of a Malpighian Body (Renal Corpuscle):

List-I (Part)List-II (Anatomical Identity)
(A) Glomerulus(I) Double-walled epithelial cup enclosing the capillary tuft
(B) Bowman's capsule(II) Tuft of capillaries formed by afferent arteriole
(C) Malpighian body(III) Glomerulus together with Bowman's capsule

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.solution: Glomerulus: Capillary network; Bowman's capsule: Double-walled cup enclosing glomerulus; Malpighian corpuscle / Renal corpuscle: The functional filtration unit composed of both Glomerulus and Bowman's capsule.

questions.question: The descending limb of the loop of Henle is:
options: Permeable to water but impermeable to electrolytes
Impermeable to water and permeable to electrolytes
Impermeable to both water and electrolytes
Actively transporting sodium ions out into cortex
questions.solution: The descending limb of Henle's loop is permeable to water but almost impermeable to electrolytes. Water diffuses out into the hypertonic medullary interstitium, concentrating the tubular fluid as it moves downward.

questions.question: The ascending limb of the loop of Henle is:
options: Impermeable to water and permeable to electrolytes (either actively or passively)
Permeable to water and impermeable to salts
Freely permeable to both water and urea
questions.solution: The ascending limb of Henle's loop is impermeable to water. It transports electrolytes ($\text{NaCl}$) out into the medullary tissue, making the tubular filtrate progressively dilute as it ascends toward the DCT.

questions.question: Which portion of the renal tubule is lined with simple cuboidal brush-border epithelium to maximize the surface area for reabsorption?
options: Thin descending limb of loop of Henle
questions.solution: The Proximal Convoluted Tubule (PCT) is lined with simple cuboidal epithelium bearing microvilli (brush border), which increases the surface area for reabsorption of water, glucose, amino acids, and essential ions.

questions.question: During urine formation, tubular secretion of which of the following substances into the filtrate helps maintain ionic balance and blood pH?
options: Hydrogen ions ($\text{H}^+$), Potassium ions ($\text{K}^+$), and Ammonia ($\text{NH}_3$)
questions.solution: Tubular secretion involves active secretion of $\text{H}^+$, $\text{K}^+$, and ammonia into the tubular fluid (in PCT, DCT, and collecting duct), which removes excess acid/ions to maintain physiological pH and electrolyte balance.

questions.question: How much of the total cardiac output is received by both kidneys together in a resting adult human?
questions.solution: On average, $1100-1200\text{ mL}$ of blood is filtered by the kidneys per minute, which accounts for roughly one-fifth ($20-25\%$) of the total cardiac output of the heart.

questions.question: The three distinct layers forming the filtration membrane during glomerular ultrafiltration are:
options: Endothelium of glomerular capillaries, basement membrane, and podocyte epithelium of Bowman's capsule
Parietal layer of Bowman's capsule, tunica media, and PCT epithelium
Ciliated epithelium, basement membrane, and visceral pleura
questions.solution: The filtration barrier consists of: (1) endothelium of glomerular blood vessels, (2) the acellular basement membrane, and (3) the podocyte epithelium of the visceral layer of Bowman's capsule.

questions.question: A person drinks a large volume of water on a cool day without sweating. What hormonal adjustments take place in their body?
options: ADH release from neurohypophysis is suppressed, reducing water reabsorption and producing abundant dilute urine (diuresis)
questions.solution: Excess water intake dilutes body fluids, switching off hypothalamic osmoreceptors and suppressing ADH release from the posterior pituitary. As a result, water reabsorption in the DCT and collecting duct decreases, leading to diuresis.

questions.question: Which of the following nitrogenous wastes is converted from toxic ammonia via the Ornithine cycle (urea cycle) in the liver?
questions.solution: In ureotelic animals (including humans), ammonia produced by deamination is converted into less toxic urea in the liver via the Ornithine (Krebs-Henseleit) cycle and then transported via blood to kidneys for filtration.

questions.question: The collecting duct plays an important role in producing concentrated urine because it:
options: Allows large amounts of water to be reabsorbed from the filtrate under the influence of ADH and allows small amounts of urea to diffuse into the medullary interstitium
Impermeable to water under all conditions
Secretes glucose and amino acids into the urine
Absorbs all urea by active transport
questions.solution: The collecting duct extends from the cortex to the inner medulla. It allows extensive water reabsorption under ADH stimulation to concentrate urine, and permits small amounts of urea to diffuse into the medullary interstitium to sustain the osmolar gradient.

questions.question: What is the ultimate curative treatment for cases of irreversible chronic end-stage renal failure?
options: Kidney transplantation from a matched living or deceased donor
Surgical excision of the urinary bladder
questions.solution: Kidney transplantation is the ultimate definitive treatment for acute or irreversible chronic end-stage renal failure (ESRF), using a functioning kidney from an immunologically matched donor.

questions.question: Which of the following compounds is NOT normally filtered into Bowman's capsule during glomerular ultrafiltration?
questions.solution: Glomerular ultrafiltration filters almost all constituents of plasma across the slit pores except large plasma proteins (colloids) and blood cells, creating a protein-free filtrate.

questions.question:
Read the following statements:
Statement I: Sweating (perspiration) primarily serves a thermoregulatory cooling function, but also facilitates the excretion of water, $\text{NaCl}$, small amounts of urea, and lactic acid.
Statement II: Sebaceous glands eliminate sterols, hydrocarbons, and waxes through sebum, providing a protective oily covering for the skin.

Choose the correct option:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct
questions.solution: Both statements are correct according to NCERT. Sweat cools the body surface while eliminating small quantities of metabolic wastes ($\text{NaCl}$, urea, lactic acid), and sebaceous glands excrete sterols, hydrocarbons, and waxes in sebum.
